summary: Updates RFC 3161 so a time-stamping authority can name its signing certificate using ESSCertIDv2, which allows hash functions other than SHA-1. It is a small proposed-standard change to support stronger hashes.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets a time-stamp office name its ID card using a newer, stronger kind of fingerprint instead of only the old kind.

questions: time stamp protocol sha-256 certificate hash
can rfc 3161 time stamps use sha-256
what does rfc 5816 change in rfc 3161
subtitle: Lets RFC 3161 time-stamp tokens name the signing certificate with a hash other than SHA-1.

tldr.problem: RFC 3161 time-stamp tokens identify the signer's certificate with ESSCertID, which only allows SHA-1 as the hash algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: This document changes three passages of RFC 3161 so that either ESSCertID or ESSCertIDv2 (from RFC 5035) can identify the certificate, with SigningCertificateV2 used for non-SHA-1 hashes.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3161 so implementers can follow policies that phase out SHA-1; the motivation is interoperability and migration, not a new vulnerability.

today: RFC 5816 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3161. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The SHA-1 Limitation
sections.content:
The time-stamping protocol in RFC 3161 requires the CMS SignedData that signs the time-stamp token to include a signed attribute identifying the signer's certificate. That identifier was built with ESSCertID from RFC 2634, which only allows SHA-1 as the hash.

RFC 5035 introduced ESSCertIDv2, which allows any hash algorithm. This document lets RFC 3161 use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The old ID card could only use one kind of fingerprint. The new one allows other kinds.

sections.title: The Three Changes to RFC 3161
sections.content:
The RFC lists old and new text for three passages. In the request-format section, the TSA certificate referenced by the ESSCertID field in a SigningCertificate attribute, or by the ESSCertIDv2 field in a SigningCertificateV2 attribute, MUST be supplied in the response when certReq is true.

In the response-format section, the certificate identifier may be either ESSCertID or ESSCertIDv2. Verification text likewise says the signer is identified by either one.

Notes: SigningCertificateV2 MUST be used with any algorithm other than SHA-1 and SHOULD NOT be used for SHA-1. For backwards compatibility both identifiers MAY be present, and systems MAY ignore ESSCertIDv2 if RFC 5035 is not implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Wherever the old rules said the old ID card, they now say either the old or the new one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ESSCertID identifies the certificate using SHA-1. Using ESSCertIDv2 aims to let implementers comply with policies that require phasing out all uses of SHA-1.

The update is motivated by interoperability and migration to other hash algorithms rather than by mitigating new security issues. The document also incorporates the security considerations of RFC 5035.
sections.plainLanguage: This is about moving to a stronger fingerprint, not about fixing a new hole.
